Upadeśasāhasrī
(‘[a treatise of] a thousand teachings’)
------------------------------------------
A theoretical treatise on any system of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् is generally called ‘prakaraṇa’. Among the several praka-raṇas on Advaita Vedānta written by शङ्कर (A.

-820), the Upadeśa-sāhasrī is also one, and, a very important one at that.
It is a fairly big work and consists of two sections known as Gadyaprabandha (Prose Section) and Padyaprabandha (Metrical Section).
The former has 116 sections divided into three prakaraṇas and the latter 675 verses spread over nineteen prakaraṇas.
Though it is universally accepted that the Metrical Section is a genuine work of शङ्कर, there are differences of opinion regarding the authorship of the Prose Section.
GADYAPRABANDHA (Prose Section)
This section is divided into three parts, each being called a prakaraṇa. They are: Śiṣyabodhavidhiprakaraṇa; Kūṭasthādvayātmabodhaprakaraṇa; Parisaṅkhyānaprakaraṇa.
In the first prakaraṇa, the आचार्य (spiritual teacher) cites many scriptures like the उपनिषद्स् and the Bhagavadgītā to show the ultimate unity of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with परमात्मन् and thus remove his अज्ञान (nescience).
In the second prakaraṇa, the लोगिच् of avasthātrayaviveka—discrimination as applied to the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् (jāgrat or waking state, स्वप्न or dreaming and सुषुप्ति or deep sleep state)—is used to prove the existence of the jīvātman as pure-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
The third prakaraṇa deals with repeated meditation on the truths discovered in the first two viz., the separation of the जीव from the body-मिन्द् complex and its ultimate identity with परमात्मन् or ब्रह्मन्.
The contents of these three sections practically correspond to the three aspects of advaitic sādhana, viz., śravaṇa (listening to the teachings of Vedānta), मनन (deep reflection on the same) and nidi-dhyāsana (meditation on the आत्मन्).
PADYAPRABANDHA (Metrical Section)
A very brief summary of the nineteen prakaraṇas may now be given:
Prakaraṇa 1 (26 verses) (Upodghātaprakaraṇa)
Ajñāna (nescience) leads to identification with the body. This leads to the performance of कर्म, experiencing its results, and rebirth. This is called सṁसार or transmigration. Hence the destruction of this सṁसार by destroying अज्ञान is necessary. The science of ब्रह्मन् or ब्रह्मविद्या is therefore taken up to destroy this सṁसार.
Prakaraṇa 2 (4 verses) (Pratiṣedhaprakaraṇa)
This section deals with the assertion of the existence of the आत्मन् by denying the body-मिन्द् complex as not being one’s real nature.
Prakaraṇa 3 (4 verses) (Īśvarātmaprakaraṇa)
This teaches that the understanding of oneself, the आत्मन्, being actually the परमात्मन्, is itself विद्या (knowledge) which dispels अविद्या (ignorance).
Prakaraṇa 4 (5 verses) (Tattvajñānasvabhāvaprakaraṇa)
Identification with the body is bondage. The awareness that one is the spirit, beyond it, is लिबेरतिओन्. This is the gist of this section.
Prakaraṇa 5 (5 verses) (Buddhyaparādhaprakaraṇa)
Not accepting आत्मज्ञान by the बुद्धि (the intellect), thinking that it leads to the giving up of the karmas prescribed for one’s वर्ण and आश्रम, is the real aparādha (mistake) committed by the बुद्धि. This can be rectified by retaining the ‘I-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्,’ to the exclusion of all that is not “I”. Then one experiences directly that one is परमात्मन्.
Prakaraṇa 6 (6 verses) (Viśeṣāpohaprakaraṇa)
When a man loses his hand, his sense of ‘I-ness’ in that is lost. Similarly if one can drop off all the adjectives or qualities that really do not belong to one’s essential nature, he will realise that he, as the knower, is the आत्मन्.
Prakaraṇa 7 (7 verses) (Buddhyārūḍhaprakaraṇa)
The आत्मन् knows everything through the बुद्धि (intellect) in which its चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is reflected. It is this साक्षी-चैतन्य (supervisory चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) that is the आत्मन्, the same as ब्रह्मन्.
Prakaraṇa 8 (6 verses) (Mativilāpanaprakaraṇa)
Given in the form of a dialogue between the आत्मन् and the मिन्द्, this section teaches that all the apparent activities of the jīvātman are due to its wrong association with the मिन्द्. In its essential nature, the jīvātman is really the आत्मन्, pure and unattached.
Prakaraṇa 9 (9 verses) (Sūkṣmatāvyāpitāprakaraṇa)
This section describes that the आत्मन् is extremely sūkṣma (subtle) and also sarvavyāpi (all-pervading) by using Upaniṣadic type of लोगिच्.
Prakaraṇa 10 (14 verses) (Dṛśisvarūpaparamārthadarśanaprakaraṇa)
The आत्मन् is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, of the nature of dṛk (the seer) and has no object to be known. He is one without a second. This is the main teaching of this prakaraṇa.
Prakaraṇa 11 (16 verses) (Īkṣitṛtvaprakaraṇa)
This section declares that चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is the natural and essential characteristic of the आत्मन्.
Prakaraṇa 12 (19 verses) (Prakāśaprakaraṇa)
It is due to sunlight that one sees one’s own body and not due to the light of the body itself since it has no light of its own. Similarly the मिन्द् that appears as the conscious knower, appears so only due to the reflection of the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in it.
Prakaraṇa 13 (27 verses) (Acakṣuṣṭvaprakaraṇa)
This section tries to prove that the आत्मन् in his essential nature is beyond the senses, vital airs, मिन्द्, intellect, and even the body. He is eternal, ever pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. Due to इग्नोरन्चे, people identify themselves with these non-Self items and suffer.
Prakaraṇa 14 (50 verses) (Svapnasmṛtiprakaraṇa)
This section proves that the आत्मन् is draṣṭṛ (the seer) and is the ever-present reality. Everything else is दृश्य, the seen, and hence non-eternal.
Prakaraṇa 15 (54 verses) (Nānyadanyatprakaraṇa)
If ब्रह्मन् and जीव are different and if जीव becomes ब्रह्मन्, then it dies, giving rise to ब्रह्मन्. But who is it that becomes ब्रह्मन्, if it were not already so? Hence one has to accept that the जीव has always been ब्रह्मन्. This is the gist of this section.
Prakaraṇa 16 (74 verses) (Pārthivaprakaraṇa)
The आत्मन् is the jñātṛ, the knower; all else, including the body-मिन्द् complex is the jñeya (the known). They—the body, the senses, the मिन्द् and the intellect—are all lighted up by the light of the आत्मन्. That is why they are able to function. This is the summary of this prakaraṇa.
Prakaraṇa 17 (89 verses) (Saṁyaṅmatiprakaraṇa)
This section emphasises that the greatest benefit one can get in life is from आत्मज्ञान or knowledge of the आत्मन्. This again is possible only through the वेदस्. The nature of this knowledge is that one is eternal, pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
Prakaraṇa 18 (233 verses) (Tattvamasiprakaraṇa)
This is the longest section, culminating in the highest philosophy of Advaita Vedānta, by a detailed exposition of the mahāvākya tat-tvam-asi (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7 to 6.16.3).
Prakaraṇa 19 (28 verses) (Bheṣajaprayogaprakaraṇa)
Also known as Ātmamanassaṁvāda-prakaraṇa, it is cast in the form of a conversation between the Self and the मिन्द्, the former advising the latter about the true nature of himself.
On the whole, this is a comprehensive and authentic treatise of Advaita Vedānta.
Rāmatīrtha (17th Century A. D.) has written a lucid commentary called Padayojanikā on the whole work.
Two more glosses—by Ānandajñāna and Bodhanidhi—are known to exist though not printed till now.

Upanayana
(‘additional eye’)
------------------------------------------
What is Saṁskāra?
Hinduism declares that मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from the cycle of birth and death is the final goal of life. It is the same as God-realisation, resulting in the enjoyment of eternal bliss. Whatever effort is put forth in that direction is called ‘sādhana’. Our body and our मिन्द् are the chief instruments in this endeavour. Saṁskāra is nothing but the process of purifying and refining these instruments, making them fit for sādhana.
The word ‘saṁskāra’ literally means ‘to do well’. A block of stone when subjected to ‘saṁskāra’ by an expert sculptor becomes a lovely image. Similarly rice, sugar and milk get converted into a delicious pudding in the hands of an expert cook.
Basic materials like the block of stone, or, rice, sugar and milk, are called ‘prakṛti’. When the stone-block is broken into pieces or rice becomes putrefied or milk gets sour, they become ‘vikṛti’ (‘deformed’), become useless. We want saṁskṛti and not vikṛti. We want ‘saṁskāra’ which can convert ‘prakṛti’ into ‘saṁskṛti’ and not its opposite, ‘vikāra’ (distortion, deformation).
Sixteen Saṁskāras
Such सṁस्कारस् (called ‘sacraments’) that purify and refine a human being, making him fit for the life here and here-after, are sixteen. Hence the term ‘Ṣoḍaśa-सṁस्कारस्’ (ṣoḍaśa = 16). Among them उपनयन, विवाह (marriage) and अन्त्येष्टि (death-rites) are the most important ones.
Meaning of the Word ‘Upanayana’
‘Upanayana’ means ‘leading’ the disciple to the गुरु or the Vedic teacher (upa = near; nayana = leading, taking). Or, it can also mean providing him with an ‘additional eye,’ the ‘eye of knowledge and wisdom’ (upa = additional, nayana = eye). That is, in addition to the two physical eyes he already has, to give him a third eye, that of knowledge and wisdom, through proper एदुचतिओन्. Consequently, the sacrament of the beginning of formal एदुचतिओन् too, has been called by the same name, i.e., ‘upanayana’.
‘Mauñjībandhana’ and ‘Brahmopadeśa’ are two other terms sometimes used to denote this sacrament. Since a girdle made of the muñja grass is tied round the waist of the boy undergoing the उपनयन ceremony, to support the kaupīna or loin-cloth, the ceremony itself is termed ‘Mauñjībandhana’.
The word ‘Brahma’ stands for the वेदस् as also for the Gāyatrīmantra which contains their quintessence. Since, in this saṁskāra, the Gāyatrīmantra is taught to the novice, the word ‘Brahmopadeśa’ is quite an appropriate expression for the rite also.
Important Steps of Upanayana
The novice undergoing उपनयन is called ‘vaṭu’. The prescribed age-limit for the vaṭu is between 7 and 16 years. It is best to perform उपनयन in the spring season (around March-April).
There are quite a few injunctions and steps in the process of the उपनयन ceremony. A few of them—the more important ones—may be set out here.
On the day prior to the उपनयन, the parents of the vaṭu should perform the worship of गणेश and the family deity.
On the day of the उपनयन, the vaṭu and his मोथेर् are to eat from the same leaf-plate. It is for the last time that they can eat like this. It signifies the end of the childhood days of the vaṭu and a life of unbridled conduct. Hereafter he cannot act and behave as he likes, but should subject himself to socio-religious norms of conduct.
Then, he has to get his head shaven, leaving a śikhā (tuft of hair) at the appropriate place, take bath and wear a new set of dress comprising kaupīna (loin-cloth), dhoti and valli (upper cloth). A girdle made of muñja grass also should be worn round the waist. It is this that is technically called mauñjībandhana. This indicates the beginning of a life of ब्रह्मचर्य or self-control, of which celibacy is the most important aspect.
Next comes the wearing of the यज्ञोपवीत or the sacred thread. The आचार्य (chief priest) makes the vaṭu wear it with appropriate mantras so that it hangs from the left shoulder to the right loin.
This sacred thread comprises three strands of strings and the knot resembles a cow in the sitting posture. At the time of the उपनयन a small piece of कृष्णाजिन (skin of a black antelope) is also tied to this sacred thread.
In the ancient days people used to wear the skin of a black antelope or an upper cloth during yajñas or sacrifices. The यज्ञोपवीत is a remnant of that practice. When the vaṭu wears it, he should think, ‘From today my life is like a यज्ञ or sacrifice. I will dedicate it to the welfare and service of the society!’ The three strands stand for the three वेदस् thereby reminding him that he has to study them and incorporate their message in his life. They may also represent purity and control of body, speech and मिन्द्, which again should be dedicated to the service of the society.
The next step is holding the दण्ड or the staff made of palāśa wood (Butea frondoza).
Actually the vaṭu is expected to keep it throughout his student-life as an inseparable companion. It stands for दम or control of the sense-organs at the psychological level. In his day-to-day life at the गुरुकुल, it helps him to take care of the cows of the household and also comes in handy in times of dangers as a weapon for self-protection.
After the vaṭu circumambulates the sacred fire and offers sacrificial fuel into it, the आचार्य administers him certain vows. They are: performing आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water with certain mantras) before any religious rite, control of speech, avoiding sleep during the day and offering fuel sticks into the sacred fire and so on.
Then comes ‘Sāvitrī Upadeśa,’ the heart of the whole sacrament. It means imparting the Gāyatrīmantra. ‘Savitṛ’ or ‘Savitā’ means God the creator. He is identified with the sun. He is the Supreme Lord residing in the heart of the sun. Hence the real name of the मन्त्र is ‘Sāvitrīmantra’. Since it was revealed to the sage विश्वामित्र, for the first time in the Vedic metre known as the गायत्री, the मन्त्र itself has been identified with it and has popularly come to be known as the ‘Gāyatrīmantra’. The आचार्य has to teach it to the vaṭu, little by little, with proper intonation until he picks it up completely.
Next comes the offering of the fuel sticks into the duly consecrated fire (that has already been prepared by the आचार्य) with proper mantras signifying prayers for long life, brilliance, intellectual acumen, general competence, name and fame as also (in course of time) good offspring.
Last comes the begging of ड़ोओद् by the vaṭu from his own मोथेर् and other elderly ladies of the family. Since he has to beg his ड़ोओद् as long as he lives in the गुरुकुल, this ritual begging is a trial run as it were, for it. The ड़ोओद् got by begging is to be offered to the आचार्य first and consume only that given to him as his share.
SANDHYĀVANDANA
Meaning of the Term
The junction between night and day (i.e., dawn) and that between day and night (i.e., dusk) are called ‘sandhyā’. The former is known as ‘prātassandhyā’ and the latter as ‘sāyaṁsandhyā’. The worship of सूर्य (the sun) to be performed during these two periods is called ‘Sandhyā-vandana’ (‘obeisance to the Sun-god during the periods of सन्ध्या’). In addition one more is added, the ‘mādhyāhnika’, a rite that is to be performed during noon when the sun is right above our head.
The vaṭu who has undergone the उपनयन ceremony, as also the होउसे-holders (among the dvijas or those belonging to the first three castes), are expected to perform this सन्ध्या ritual three times a day, as a sacred duty.
These three—the prātassandhyā, the mādhyāhnika and the sāyaṁsandhyā—have many steps in common. However, in practice, only the first and the last have survived. The scriptures have provided for this modification.
Various Steps
After taking bath and wearing the traditional religious dress (dhoti and chadar or uttarīya) one should apply the religious marks (like the विभूति or the ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र) as per one’s family traditions, on the forehead, and sit on the seat (kept aside and to be used only for such religious purposes). Though there are differences in the procedure and the various steps to be followed, as per differing traditions, the six steps common to all will be delineated here. The detailed procedure has to be learnt from the family priest or the elders in the family.
These six steps are: आचमन, prāṇā-yāma, मार्जन, arghyapradāna, गायत्री-जप and sūryopasthāna.
a) Ācamana
Ācamana is the ceremonial sipping of water from the right hand cupped in the shape of the face of a cow, to the chanting of appropriate mantras like ‘Keśavāya स्वाहा’ and touching specified parts of the body for ritual purification. This आचमन is a general purificatory act that precedes every religious undertaking.
b) Prāṇāyāma
Prāṇāyāma is control of the prāṇic energy through the regulation of the breathing process as detailed in the works on योग. पूरक (inhalation), कुम्भक (retention) and रेचक (exhalation) are its three steps. The Gāyatrīmantra along with the व्याहृतिस् is used in प्राणायाम to keep time. प्राणायाम helps in the control of मिन्द् also.
c) Mārjana
Literally, ‘mārjana’ means cleansing or purifying. It consists of sprinkling of water on specified parts of the body with the मन्त्र ‘āpo hiṣṭhā....’ This process will make the body ceremonially pure and fit for the ritualistic act.
d) Arghyapradāna
Any object fit for being offered in ritualistic worship is ‘arghya’. However, in a more technical sense, it is the offering of water taken in the two hands cupped together, by repeating the Gāyatrīmantra and addressing the Sun-god (i.e., Savitā or God the creator, in the orb of the sun). This is just to show our gratitude to the Sun-god who is our primary life-support.
e) Gāyatrījapa
This is the most important part of the सन्ध्या ritual. Its primary steps are: करन्यास, अङ्गन्यास, ध्यान and जप.
‘Nyāsa’ means ‘to keep or to place’. It is aimed at filling the fingers of the hand and other limbs like the head and heart with the divine power of the deities.
Dhyāna is meditation on the deity as per the detailed description given in the hymn (called ‘dhyānaśloka’) while repeating it. The goddess गायत्री within the orb of the sun is the deity here.
After ध्यान comes जप or repetition of the Gāyatrīmantra. While doing जप, ध्यान on the form of the goddess should be continued. It is better to repeat the मन्त्र 1008 times, or at least 108 times per sitting.
f) Sūryopasthāna
Repeating the prayer addressed to the deity गायत्री (in the orb of the sun) in the standing posture, facing the sun, is ‘sūryopasthāna’ (upasthāna = standing). This is the last rite of bidding farewell to the goddess after having invoked her and satiated her through जप.
Apart from the sun, the mountain मेरु is sometimes described as her abode.
UPĀKARMA
In the ancient days, the brahmacārins (Vedic students) used to stay in the houses of their teachers and study the वेदस्. After a few months of study and a short holiday, when they resumed their study, they were expected to perform a short ritual called ‘upākarma,’ signifying the restarting of their studies. The word ‘upā-कर्म’ means ‘upakrama’ or ‘prārambha’, or beginning.
Now-a-days, it has remained just as an annual ritual. The procedure comprises the following steps: सङ्कल्प (religious resolve), worship of गणपति, oblations to nine deities like सावित्री, ब्रह्मा and श्रद्धा, होम with a mixture of barley and curds with some specific mantras from the Ṛgveda, wearing of a new यज्ञोपवीत and discarding the old one, preferably in the waters of a river or a tank.
The same मन्त्र and procedure for changing the यज्ञोपवीत given here can be used at other times also, to discard a worn-out or a dirty or a broken one and wear a new one.
GĀYATRĪ-मन्त्र-JAPA
What is गायत्री?
It is known as ‘Gāyatrī’ since it protects (= trāyate) one who chants it (= gāyantam) correctly as per the rules of Vedic intonation. This is the etymological definition of the word.
It is also called ‘Sāvitrīmantra’ since it is a prayer addressed to Savitṛ or God the creator. The Sun is also called Savitṛ or Savitā, because it is due to him (or the power of God in him) that the whole world and all of us, are able to live.
This मन्त्र was revealed for the first time to the sage विश्वामित्र, in a new metre called ‘Gāyatrī’. Hence the मन्त्र itself came to be known as ‘Gāyatrīmantra’. It is also called ‘Sāvitrī-मन्त्र’ since it concerns the deity Savitṛ.
The मन्त्र and Its Meaning
The first part of the मन्त्र comprises the three व्याहृतिस्:
Om bhūr-bhuvas-suvaḥ (Oṁ, bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ).
When the गायत्री is used for prāṇā-yāma, the number of व्याहृतिस् is increased from 3 to 7.
Literally ‘vyāhṛti’ means ‘uttering’. ब्रह्मा the creator, is said to have uttered these at the beginning of च्रेअतिओन्. Hence the appellation ‘vyāhṛtis’.
The second part is the सावित्रीमन्त्र:
tat savitur-vareṇyam, bhargo devasya dhīmahi, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ॥
Sometimes, a third part called ‘Gāyatrī-śiras’ is also added. Its use also is in the process of प्राणायाम. It is:
Om āpo jyotī raso’mṛtam brahma bhūrbhuvassuvarom ॥`
However, in the मन्त्र used for जप, only the three व्याहृतिस् and the सावित्री-मन्त्र are utilised.
A general summary of the मन्त्र may now be given:
We meditate upon the divine effulgence of Savitā (God, the creator of the three worlds, the earth, the हेअवेन् and the intervening space as indicated by the three व्याहृतिस्) signified by the प्रणव or ओङ्कार (and existing in the orb of the sun). May he impel our intellects in the right direction (i.e., towards himself)!
Whatever we want to achieve in our life, the first and foremost requirement is that our intellect, our understanding, must be in an excellent form! Repetition of the Gāyatrīmantra with faith and reverence will help not only in cleansing the मिन्द् but also in achieving greater concentration.
The mode and method of its repetition must be learnt from a competent teacher.
Puraścaraṇa
Puraścaraṇa is the technical name given to a particular (ceremonial) mode of repeating the Gāyatrīmantra in order to secure certain special fruits or results. The following are the usual steps involved in it:
Daily rituals like the सन्ध्या-vandana, worship of the goddess गायत्री, जप of Gāyatrīmantra, होम (fire ritual), तर्पण (offering of water ceremonially) and feeding of the ब्राह्मणस्.
It should be undertaken, however, under the guidance of experts.

Upakosala
------------------------------------------
Upakosala—also known as काम-lāyana—was a disciple of the sage Satyakāma Jābāla. He served his गुरु for twelve years, tending his sacred fires with great care and devotion. Though Satyakāma Jābāla educated and sent away his other disciples, he did not condescend to teach उपकोसल. Even the sympathetic intervention of his wife in favour of उपकोसल had no effect. Then उपकोसल started ड़स्तिन्ग् out of dejection. The Vedic fires which he had devotedly served, took pity on him and taught him that प्राण (the life force) and the bliss one experiences in the region of the heart are ब्रह्मन्.
Later on, Satyakāma discovered that उपकोसल had been taught by the Vedic fires. He completed the same by teaching him about the आत्मन्, the seer in the eye (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10 to 4.15).

upavāsa
(‘fasting’)
------------------------------------------
Upavāsa or ड़स्तिन्ग् as a spiritual discipline or as a part of religious rites or even as an expiation for sins is found in all the major religions of the world. हिन्दुइस्म् has plenty of it.
Fasting undertaken voluntarily and willingly helps to discipline both the body and the मिन्द्. Along with ड़स्तिन्ग्, worship of one’s deity, repetition of the divine name, observance of mauna or silence, keeping vigil in the night as also chanting of hymns and devotional singing are to be undertaken.
Generally ड़स्तिन्ग् means avoiding cooked ड़ोओद्. Uncooked ड़ोओद् like fruits and milk is permitted. However, total abstinence from all kinds of ड़ोओद् is also recommended to those who are strong enough to withstand it.
If ड़स्तिन्ग् is to be undertaken as a part of प्रायश्चित्त or expiation, it can be of three kinds: एकभक्त (eating only once in the day); नक्त (eating only once, at night); and, अयाचित (taking the ड़ोओद् that is brought unasked).
Old and weak persons, patients and little children are not expected to fast.

Upapurāṇas
------------------------------------------
Ancient legends preserved in the collective memory of the Hindus gradually took the shape of the Mahāpurāṇas. Tradition enumerates them as eighteen and ascribes their authorship to the sage वेदव्यास.
Along with these Mahāpurāṇas, there gradually grew up another mass of literature, similar to them. These works came to be known as उपपुराणस्. Though assigned to वेदव्यास as the author, they are obviously the works of different sages composed over a few centuries.
The lists of the eighteen उपपुराणस् given in different पुराणस् vary considerably.
A few of these उपपुराणस् may now be described briefly:
Ādi Upapurāṇa
The printed version as available now is assigned to the period A.

. This contains the story of कृष्ण in detail.
Bhaviṣyottara Upapurāṇa
Apart from some interesting stories, it gives descriptions of the code of conduct according to धर्म, to be followed by all.
Brahmottara Upapurāṇa
It appears to be an appendix of the Brahmapurāṇa. Comprising 3000 verses it describes the greatness of the river known as Balajā in the country of Mārvār.
Bṛhad-धर्म Upapurāṇa
This is a fairly big work. According to it, the whole च्रेअतिओन् depends upon शिव and शक्ति. Stories of धर्मव्याध, Śrī राम, descent of the गङ्गा river, lives of great sages like व्यास and वाल्मीकि, of avatāras of विष्णु, varṇāśrama-dharmas, greatness of the Mahābhārata, one’s duties towards parents and other elders, the need for a good and efficient king to rule over a country and a host of other topics have been dealt with here.
Devībhāgavata Upapurāṇa
This is a voluminous work, containing the story of महिषासुर being killed by the देवी. A lot of material connected with rituals and worship is also included.
Kālikā Upapurāṇa
This is a work devoted to the शाक्त cult. It describes the various aspects of पार्वती such as Girijā, देवी, Bhadrakālī and Kālī. A description of the temple of कामाख्या in Assam, story of दक्ष’s sacrifice, worship of the देवी and some tāntrik rites are a part of this work.
Kalki Upapurāṇa
This is considered as an appendix of Bhāgavata. Probably composed during A.

, it gives the story of कल्कि, as the tenth अवतार of विष्णु, to appear in future.
Nāradīya Upapurāṇa
This work concentrates mainly on the story of रुक्माङ्गद, a great devotee of विष्णु.
Narasiṁha Upapurāṇa
This is a comparatively ancient work assigned to the period A.

. लोमहर्षण, a disciple of वेदव्यास, taught this to the sages like Bhāradvāja at प्रयाग.
The following are the topics dealt with in this work: hymns to Lord नरसिṁह; च्रेअतिओन् of the world according to the Sāṅkhya system; origin of some मनुस् and ṛṣis; meditations on ब्रह्मा and विष्णु; greatness of the अष्टाक्षरी मन्त्र (eight-lettered मन्त्र of नारायण); 108 names of आदित्य (Sun-god); duties towards elders and superiors; construction details of the temple of नरसिṁह; evils of कलियुग; places of पिल्ग्रिमगे dedicated to विष्णु.
Puruṣottama Upapurāṇa
This upapurāṇa, still in the manuscript from, is devoted entirely to the glorification of the pilgrim centre पुरी (or Jagannātha पुरी) including the details of the worship of the deities there.
Sāmba Upapurāṇa
This is one of the few उपपुराणस् that has been printed. It probably belongs to the period A.

-800.
The principal hero of this work is Sāmba, the eldest son of Śrī कृष्ण. He is pictured as a votary of सूर्य (the Sun-god) and a propagator of the सूर्य-cult. He was responsible for bringing the Maga ब्राह्मणस्, worshippers of सूर्य, and settled them in a colony.
The subjects dealt with in this upapurāṇa are as follows: establishing the image of सूर्य and सूर्य temples; geographical details of the earth; योग; the three वेदस्; सṁन्यास; characteristics of a devotee of सूर्य; observance of vratas like रथसप्तमी; some śānti rites; a few hymns on सूर्य.
Saura Upapurāṇa
This is an appendix of the Brahma-purāṇa. It teaches that शिव and सूर्य are identical. Liṅgapūjā (worship of the शिवलिङ्ग) is described in detail.
Śiva Upapurāṇa
This is a fairly big work. The greatness of शिव is the main theme. Worship of शिव through the शिवलिङ्ग is described in detail. Other topics are: Śivasahasra-nāma; importance of ड़स्तिन्ग् and festivals; a few tāntrik practices.
Viṣṇudharma Upapurāṇa
This work contains 4000 verses spread over 105 chapters. It was probably composed during the period A.

-300.
Some of the topics dealt with are: stories of अम्बरीष and प्रह्लाद; various kinds of Vaiṣṇava vratas; descriptions of some hells; eulogy of दान (giving gifts); greatness of a true ब्राह्मण and a true क्षत्त्रिय hero; devotion to विष्णु; power of सुदर्शन discus; temples and images; some beautiful stotras or hymns; sins and means of offsetting their effects.
The Agnipurāṇa seems to have drawn upon this Upapurāṇa for some of its topics.
Viṣṇudharmottara Upapurāṇa
This is a fairly large work, almost encyclopaedic in character. It might have been composed during the period A.

to 500.
The following are some of the topics dealt with in this work: अस्त्रोनोम्य्; च्रेअतिओन्; अस्त्रोलोग्य्; śakunaśāstra or science of prognostication; कर्म and its consequences; śrāddha (obsequial rites); दान (giving gifts); राजनीति (political science); science of war; आयुर्वेद; science of मुसिच्; election of a king and his चोरोनतिओन्; duties of a king; a few magical sciences.
There is reason to believe that the Matsyapurāṇa has borrowed some chapters from this upapurāṇa.
Apart from these, many more उपपुराणस् have been discovered and also quoted in some nibandha works. Some of them are: Ekāmrapurāṇa, Yugapurāṇa, Gaṇeśapurāṇa, and Caṇḍikāpurāṇa.
There is no doubt that these upa-पुराणस् also have considerably enriched popular हिन्दुइस्म्.

Upaveda
(‘subsidiary Veda’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘veda’ means knowledge, a particular science.
Certain subsidiary fields of know-ledge which also go by the title ‘Veda’ are considered very important for the develop-ment of the human society. The are: आयुर्वेद (science of life or health); धनुर्वेद (science of war); गान्धर्व-वेद (science of मुसिच्); Śastraśāstra (science of weapons).
These four are said to be associated respectively with the four well-known वेदस्, viz., Ṛgveda, यजुर्वेद, Sāmaveda and Atharvaveda.

upādānakāraṇa
(‘material cause’)
------------------------------------------
See NIMITTA.

upādhyāya
(‘teacher [of वेदस्]’)
------------------------------------------
An उपाध्याय is a Vedic teacher who teaches the Veda or a part of it, for remuneration. He is also called adhyāpaka.
An upādhyāyā is a lady teacher of the वेदस्, whereas the wife of an उपाध्याय is known as upādhyāyānī or upādhyāyī.
Other words of similar purport are: श्रोत्रिय or chāndasa (scholar well-versed in the वेदस्); आचार्य (one who teaches the वेदस् along with their meaning); गुरु (who performs the सṁस्कारस् or the sacraments).

upāsana
(‘sitting near,’ ‘meditation’)
------------------------------------------
In general, the word उपासन means meditation.
However, in the Pāñcarātra Āgamas, it has been used in a technical sense associated with ritualistic worship. It has five aspects: abhigamana (keeping the temple clean); upādāna (collecting the materials needed for worship); ijyā (ritualistic worship); स्वाध्याय (repetition of God’s name and chanting of hymns); योग (meditation on God).

upastaraṇa
(‘act of spreading’)
------------------------------------------
In some वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, rice-cakes called पुरोडाश are used for offering into the consecrated fire. आज्य or ghee is spread below these पुरोडाश cakes before they are cut. This act of spreading is called उपस्तरण.
In Somayāgas, a little सोम juice is put into the camasas (cups) before filling them. This too is called उपस्तरण.

Upaniṣads
------------------------------------------
1. General Introduction
If there is one mass of scriptures that has inspired and sustained the Hindus over the millennia, it is the उपनिषद्स्. By advocating the ultimate triumph of the spirit over matter, of man over nature, the उपनिषद्स् have created, strengthened and preserved a great tradition of spirituality. This they have done, not only by a fearless spirit of inquiry to its logical conclusions, but also by intuitive mystical experiences beyond the ken of the intellect, these experiences almost always converging to a unitive principle. No school of thought, no religious movement, of the subsequent periods in the history of India has remained untouched by their influence, if not pervaded by them. In fact, many of these schools and movements could gain respectability or acceptance only because they trode the path lighted up by the उपनिषद्स्.
Research scholars of Indian thought have discovered the influence of the उपनिषद्स् on the religio-cultural life of other nations far beyond the boundaries of India, whether it is Japan, China and Korea in the east or Central Asia in the west.
Hindu religious tradition has always accorded the उपनिषद्स् the status of the highest authority since it has unquestioningly been accepted as Śruti, the Revealed

Word.
2

. Meaning of the Word ‘Upaniṣad’
The word ‘Upaniṣad’ is derived from the verbal root sad which has several meanings: loosening, movement and annihilation. Putting all these three senses together, the word ‘Upaniṣad’ refers to that divine knowledge or wisdom which loosens the bonds of सṁसार (transmigratory existence) of a being, annihilates his अज्ञान or the इग्नोरन्चे of his real nature, and leads him to ब्रह्मन् or God, the Absolute. The book or the scriptural work that teaches this wisdom is also called ‘Upaniṣad’.
The word may also mean ‘sitting devotedly near’. Hence it represents the ‘secret teaching, of spiritual wisdom’ imparted in private to worthy pupils, but jealously guarded from the unworthy ones.
3. Date of Composition
The orthodox view is that the उपनिषद्स् are Revealed Word. They are revealed by God himself at the commencement of each cycle of च्रेअतिओन् to the worthy few. Hence they are eternal.
However, treating them as books of spiritual wisdom, can we assign any date or period, in relation to human history as known till now? Attempts in this direction have rather been frustrating, thanks to that peculiar trait of the Hindu मिन्द् which accords much greater importance to the principle rather than to the person or the period.
The उपनिषद्स् have been an integral part of the वेदस्. Hence, a date assigned to them can as well hold good for the उपनिषद्स् also. The date of the Ṛgveda has varied from 4500 B. C. (B. G. Tilak) and 2400 B. C. (Hang) to 1200 B. C. (Max Müller). Modern European scholars assign the period 700 B. C.-600 B. C. to the उपनिषद्स् assuming a gradual evolution of the philosophical ideas from the period of the Vedic hymns to that of the आरण्यकस् and the उपनिषद्स्. B. G. Tilak, on the basis of an astronomical data provided in the Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad, has however, assigned 1900 B. C. as the date of that Upaniṣad. Hence, according to him and the scholars who concur with him, the उपनिषद्स् belong to the period 2500 B. C.—2000 B.

. Nature of Composition
From among the extant उपनिषद्स्, only ten to fifteen are considered to be the older ones. They are the basic sources of ancient Hindu philosophy.
However, do all these उपनिषद्स् teach a single system of philosophy? Or, do they contain several, mutually conflicting, systems?
The orthodox Hindu tradition has always considered the entire body of the Upaniṣadic literature as one unit (‘Śruti’) and hence teaching one philosophy. Though this philosophy may contain several aspects, they always form a homogeneous unit.
A look at the different and divergent teachings of these उपनिषद्स् does not easily convince us about the soundness of the orthodox standpoint. The traditional commentators have, however, solved this problem by sticking to one view as the teaching of the उपनिषद्स् and explaining (explaining away?) the others in a way that suits their interpretation.
Could it be that, over the centuries, many vital links have been lost, and what we now have are only fragments of the original works leading to this dichotomy of views? Though this is a plausible explanation, there is no clinching evidence to prove it.
Or, can we say that the various sages that we come across in the Upaniṣads—like गौतम आरुणि, याज्ञवल्क्य, Śveta-केतु or Raikva—were great thinkers and mystics in their own right, who have given independent views, based on their own लोगिच् and experience? The Truth, ब्रह्मन् (the Infinite, the Absolute), is too great to be known exhaustively by anyone. One can get only a glimpse of the same, like the six blind men touching the same elephant. Hence, could it not be that the views of these sages, though apparently different, reflect the several facets of the same ब्रह्मन्?
At the most, these are all intelligent guesses and may continue to remain so for quite some time!
5. Number and Classification
The number of works that go by the name ‘Upaniṣad’ and available in print today exceeds 200. The Muktikopaniṣad gives a list of 108 उपनिषद्स्. शङ्कर (A.
—820), the earliest commentator, has chosen only ten उपनिषद्स् to expound. He refers to a few more in his commentary on the Brahmasūtras. Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) has chosen, in addition, two more. Considering the ones chosen by them as more ancient and authoritative we can now list them (in the alphabetical order) as follows:
Aitareya Upaniṣad
Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
Chāndogya Upaniṣad
Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad
Jābāla Upaniṣad
Kaivalya Upaniṣad
Kaṭha Upaniṣad
Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
Kena Upaniṣad
Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
Praśna Upaniṣad
Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
Taittirīya Upaniṣad
Vajrasūcikā Upaniṣad
As regards the classification, different scholars have adopted different methods. Some have grouped them in the chronological order, considering the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka, the Chāndogya and the Taittirīya as more ancient than the Kaṭha or the Śvetāśvatara. Others have classified them according to the style of language, as उपनिषद्स् in prose or in poetry. Such methods of classification do not help us much in studying them.
Most of the उपनिषद्स्, outside the list given above, belong to a much later period in our history and were written to propagate specific cults and sects. The nomenclature ‘Upaniṣad’ was conveniently added to them to gain respectability, acceptance and authority in the orthodox circles or among the followers. However, it must be conceded that these उपनिषद्स् also, though sectarian in character, have contributed quite a lot to the propagation of popular religion and एथिच्स् as also to the maintenance of the Vedāntic spirit among the people.
These minor उपनिषद्स् are sometimes grouped as follows:
Vedānta Upaniṣads
Śaiva Upaniṣads
Śākta Upaniṣads
Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads
Yoga Upaniṣads
Saṁnyāsa Upaniṣads
The Vedānta उपनिषद्स् follow the beaten track of the major उपनिषद्स् as far as the general principles are concerned. The Śaiva, the शाक्त and the Vaiṣṇava उपनिषद्स् deal with the respective cults of शिव, देवी and विष्णु. The योग उपनिषद्स् supply a lot of information about हठयोग and राजयोग based on the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि and other works. The सṁन्यास उपनिषद्स् deal exclusively with मोनस्तिचिस्म्, its ideals and practices.
6. Sanskrit Commentaries
By its very definition, an Upaniṣad is an esoteric work, recondite in nature and spirit. The language is archaic. Many of the concepts, being closely allied to the sacrificial religion of the Saṁhitās and the ब्राह्मणस्, are unintelligible to us, removed as we are, by millennia, from those rituals or ideas. Hence it is impossible to understand them, much less, get a consistent view of them, without an authoritative and reliable commentary. शङ्कर (A.

-820) is the earliest and the first to comment upon them. His bhāṣyas or commentaries, further elucidated by the ṭīkās or glosses of आनन्दगिरि (13th century) are invaluable source books to unlock the wisdom of the उपनिषद्स्.
Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) has not commented upon any of the उपनिषद्स् though he has tried to amplify some of their concepts in his Vedārthasaṅgraha. Raṅga-rāmānuja (circa A.
) has completed the work by commenting on all the major उपनिषद्स्. Madhva (A.
-1276) has written brief commentaries on all the ten ancient उपनिषद्स् upon which some like Rāghavendra Tīrtha (A.

-1671) have written glosses.
Some commentators have chosen to write only on certain उपनिषद्स्. The Īśāvāsyopaniṣad has attracted the attention of many scholars like Brahmānanda सरस्वती, Śaṅkarānanda (14th cent.), Uvaṭārya (11th cent.) as also Vedānta-deśika (A.

-1370) who have not chosen to comment on the other उपनिषद्स्. Rāghavendra Tīrtha has commented on the Īśa, Kena, Kaṭha, Praśna, Muṇḍaka and Māṇḍūkya following Madhva’s line of interpretation. A later writer, Upaniṣad Brahma Yogīndra, has done remarkable work by commenting on most of the minor उपनिषद्स्.
7. Philosophy of the Upaniṣads
The thought current of the उपनिषद्स् is, in a way, a continuation of that in the ब्राह्मणस् and the आरण्यकस्. However, the trend is definitely against ritualism and strongly favours upāsanā (meditation) and ज्ञान (knowledge).
In the more philosophical portions of the उपनिषद्स्, the discussions generally centre round the fundamental cause of the world, if there is one, and its nature as also its evolution into this world. This cause is usually called ‘Brahman.’
As against this, there is a parallel mode of enquiry, into the existence or otherwise, of a permanent subjective entity behind the body-मिन्द् complex. This is called ‘ātman’ (the Self or the सोउल्).
Is this आत्मन् one or many? Is it finite in size or infinite? Is it identical with ब्रह्मन् or different? Though the उपनिषद्स् discuss these questions, there does not appear to be a single answer. Different viewpoints seem to exist. However, the orthodox Vedāntic schools struggle to present only one view as the right one to the exclusion of the others.
Destiny of the living beings here and hereafter, including some eschatological questions, form another topic of the उपनिषद्स्. इग्नोरन्चे of one’s real nature as the cause of bondage and its eradication through the practice of certain virtues like self-control and speaking the truth are also touched upon.
A brief summary of these teachings may now be given.
BRAHMAN
The basic cause of the universe, the cause of all causes, is called ‘Brahman’ by the उपनिषद्स्. आत्मन्, Sat, अक्षर. आकाश and Bhūmā are the other appellations used for this ब्रह्मन्. The world rises out of him, is supported by him and gets dissolved back into him. He is omniscient, omnipotent and omnipresent. He is greater than the greatest, smaller than the smallest and is also the inmost Self of all. He is immanent in this world even as salt is, in saline water. He is beyond all wants and limitations. He is the lord as well as the substratum of the whole च्रेअतिओन्. He sees, hears and knows although none can see or hear or know him. He is the very personification of all the great virtues to their perfection. It is he who responds to the prayers of his votaries and grants them whatever they seek. He is the ultimate goal of all.
To facilitate meditation upon him, the उपनिषद्स् sometimes describe him as a पुरुष (the divine being in the human form), bright and brilliant, of golden hue, with all parts of his body of golden colour and his eyes resembling a fully bloomed red lotus. Fire is his head, the sun and the मोओन् are his eyes, the quarters are his ears, the वेदस् are his speech and the earth is his feet. Sometimes he is also described as having thousand heads, thousand eyes and thousand feet, thereby stressing his omnipresent cosmic form. This form recommended for meditation is the Aupaniṣada-पुरुष (the Being described in the उपनिषद्स्).
ĀTMAN
When a person dies, is there anything in him that survives and continues to live on? What is that, impelled by which, the senses and the मिन्द् of a living person are active? Such inquiries by the sages of the उपनिषद्स् have led to the establishment of the आत्मन्, the सोउल् or the Self, as the abiding spirit behind the body and the मिन्द् of every living being.
This आत्मन् is neither born nor does he die with the birth and the death of the body. He is unborn and eternal. He is different from the body, the senses, the vital airs, the मिन्द् and the ego-sense and is ever free. All of them are enlivened by him, made to work by him, for him. The defects and the infirmities in them, or even their loss, can never affect him.
However, it is also a fact of experience that this आत्मन् has been encased and bound in this corporeal frame and has lost much of his freedom. In this state, he is called ‘jīvātman’ or simply the ‘jīva’. The answer to the question as to why and how he has come to such a pass is ‘karma,’ the inexorable consequence of his past actions. For the question, how and when the very first कर्म started this chain of bondage, there is no answer, since the उपनिषद्स् accept च्रेअतिओन् as an eternal process, without beginning or end.
His involvement in the cycle of birth and death, and consequent suffering, has been called ‘saṁsāra.’ मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from this bondage of सṁसार has been presented before him as the goal of his life. And, this can be achieved by ज्ञान or knowledge and, भक्ति or devotion, which includes upāsanā or meditation. कर्म or action as prescribed in the scriptures is an aid to this मोक्ष.
CREATION
Though ब्रह्मन् is the permanent substratum of this world and आत्मन् is our essential nature, we cannot ignore this world in which we live and move and have our being as it were. For all practical purposes it is very real to us. And, even our struggles or attempts for मोक्ष have to take place only in this world. Hence, it is necessary to know about it, how it came into being, how it is sustained now and its ultimate destiny.
In the beginning, ब्रह्मन् alone—also called ‘Ātman’ or ‘Sat’—existed, as the one without a second. He decided to become many. He then created out of himself, आकाश (sky or space or ether), वायु (air), अग्नि or तेजस् (fire), ap (water) and पृथ्वी (earth). A permutation and combination of these five elements, with ब्रह्मन् associated at every stage, has resulted in this world. Later, ब्रह्मन् entered into this च्रेअतिओन् as the antar-yāmin or the inner controlling spirit.
According to other descriptions, the original substances created were only three (tejas, ap and अन्न or earth) or even two, rayi (moon or अन्न or matter) and प्राण (sun or fire or energy or spirit). By a combination of these, in different proportions, this world came into being. It is ever under his control. Nay, it is non-different from him.
Even after being created out of—or, emerging out of—Brahman, this world continues to be in him. It will merge back in him at the time of प्रलय or dissolution.
With regard to the relationship between ब्रह्मन् and the world, two views seem to exist in the उपनिषद्स्. According to one view—known as Saprapañcavāda—since the world is an evolute of ब्रह्मन्, it is also ब्रह्मन्. The other view—called as Niṣprapañcavāda—denies the world an existence of its own and asserts the existence of ब्रह्मन् alone.
BONDAGE AND LIBERATION
Some उपनिषद्स् picture the jīvātman and the परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self, ब्रह्मन् as the indwelling spirit) as two birds perching on the same tree (the body). The former eats the fruits of the tree (results of कर्म)—some sweet and some bitter—and experiences joy and sorrow. The latter is sitting majestically, ever calm and collected, never touching those fruits. When the jīvātman realises the greatness of परमात्मन्, he becomes free from all sorrow and suffering.
Though the question, how the everfree आत्मन् became the जीव, has not been answered by the उपनिषद्स्, they have given several modes of sādhana or spiritual exercises by which the जीव can recover his original state.
A sādhaka or a spiritual aspirant should first cultivate certain moral and ethical virtues as the first step. Through discrimination he should understand that the Vedic rituals can never lead him to the eternal Truth and hence renounce them. He must be ever ready to reject the प्रेयस् (the pleasant) and choose the श्रेयस् (the good). By eschewing evil conduct and by practising self-control, he should turn back his मिन्द् from outside, into himself, the region of the heart, the seat of the आत्मन्, and meditate on it. He should show compassion to all the living beings. He should try to give them what they need and should never be greedy. He must be vigilant forever and should always speak the truth and act according to धर्म or righteousness, by following the scriptural injunctions. Study of the उपनिषद्स्, performing austerities and observing ब्रह्मचर्य or celibacy are also invaluable aids in his sādhana.
He should approach a competent गुरु or spiritual teacher in all humility and learn the truth about the आत्मन् from him, through proper questioning and sevā or service to him.
The उपनिषद्स् make it incumbent on the गुरु to teach spiritual wisdom to a worthy disciple, after testing him if necessary.
The disciple should then practise मनन (reflection) and निदिध्यासन (meditation) on the आत्मन् which will result in anubhūti or realisation.
What is the nature of the spiritual experience that an aspirant gets when he realises the आत्मन्? He sees all beings in himself and himself in all. Hence he feels neither special attraction nor repulsion for others. Behind every thought of his, he is able to feel the power of the आत्मन्, the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He clearly perceives that all the bonds of his heart which had him tied down to this mundane existence, have broken down. He experiences great joy and bliss within himself. When he directs his attention outside, there too he sees the same spirit, the आत्मन्, the ब्रह्मन्.
The bliss he experiences is incomparably superior to any other happiness one can get in this world. And he will never have any type of regret for anything in life. He may even roam about the world in a joyous state, declaring his experiences for the benefit of others.
When such a one, the jīvanmukta (one who is liberated even while living here in this body), gives up his body, what happens to him?
According to one view, his physical body and the subtle body disintegrate at death and get absorbed into the five elements. And, he gets merged in ब्रह्मन्, like a river entering into the ocean. Losing his separate identity, he attains complete and perfect unity with ब्रह्मन्.
However, a large body of the Upaniṣadic lore propounds the theory of the liberated सोउल् travelling by the Arcirādimārga or the Bright Path (also called देवयान and उत्तरायण) to the ब्रह्मलोक (also known as सत्यलोक) and reside there permanently in infinite peace and bliss. The various stations on the path are fire, day, bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice, the year, the sun, the मोओन् and the lightning. All these actually represent the guardian deities of these stations. From the last station, the vidyut or lightning, an ‘amānava पुरुष,’ a non-human (divine) being, leads the liberated सोउल् to the ब्रह्मलोक.
Is the ब्रह्मलोक a state of inner experience or an actual world to which the liberated सोउल् repairs? Most of the उपनिषद्स् contain practically no or very scanty details. The Chāndogya (8.5.3) describes it as a world, third from this earth, wherein there are two huge lakes called Ara and Ṇya. There is also a smaller reservoir of ड़ोओद्-juice known as Airammadīya. Somasavana, a peepul tree and a city called अपराजिता, containing a golden hall are also there. The Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇopaniṣad (1.3, 4 and 5) gives a more picturesque description which adds a river Virajā, two doorkeepers (Indra and प्रजापति), a throne called Vicakṣaṇa and a couch by name Amitaujas. Five hundred celestial nymphs greet the liberated सोउल् and adorn him. The fragrance and flavour of ब्रह्मा enters him at the appropriate state of his entrance.
Anyone reaching ब्रह्मलोक will not return to mundane existence.
ESCHATOLOGY
What happens to a person who dies without realising the आत्मन्/Brahman? This question too has been discussed in the उपनिषद्स्.
Those who have performed sakāma-karmas (desire-motivated actions) or have practised lower kinds of upāsanās get their desires fulfilled. Some of them go to svargaloka स्वर्ग is mentioned in the उपनिषद्स् several times, its opposite, नरक (hell), has not been alluded to, except in one minor Upaniṣad. Sometimes, this movement is described as through the Dhūmādimārga (the path of smoke) (also called दक्षिणायन) wherein the सोउल् is led to the Candraloka (the world of मोओन्) after passing through smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the six months of the southern solstice. After exhausting the result of meritorious deeds he returns again to this earth, through the sky, rain, vegetation and living beings.
Those who know neither of these two paths, return again and again and may even be reborn at the subhuman levels, as animals and worms.
As related to this topic, ideas about कर्म and rebirth are also found in the उपनिषद्स् here and there. A doer of puṇyakarma or good deeds attains good results and a doer of pāpakarma or sinful deeds gets bad results. Hence human beings are advised not to harm anyone.
VIDYĀS OR UPĀSANĀS
An important aspect of sādhana as enunciated in the उपनिषद्स् is ‘vidyā’ or upāsanā. A man deeply devoted to—or even addicted to—the religion of yajñas or वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, has to be led gradually, first to contemplation and then to ज्ञान (knowledge or direct experience) of the आत्मन् in course of time, because that is the ultimate goal of life. And, that is the only way to मोक्ष.
These upāsanās have taken two forms. In the first group, the sādhaka is advised to imagine the various parts of a ritual and then superimpose certain ideas on them. For instance, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (

, 2) advises one to meditate upon the horse, to be offered in the अश्वमेध sacrifice, by thinking that it is प्रजापति, the Lord of beings. This upāsanā, which can be practised even by those who are not competent to perform the अश्वमेध sacrifice, gives the same fruits as the real अश्वमेध itself.
In the second group of upāsanās certain known objects like nāma (name), vāk (speech), बल (strength) or मनस् (mind) are recommended to be meditated upon as ब्रह्मन्, by imagining or discovering some similarity between that object and ब्रह्मन्. Such upāsanās gradually help the aspirant’s मिन्द् to be raised to the highest level, ब्रह्मन्, and give him the much needed spiritual experience.

8. Civilisation and Culture during the Age of the Upaniṣads
Gleaning through the various उपनिषद्स् it is possible to have a fairly good idea of the type of society that existed during the period of the उपनिषद्स्.
The country extended up to गान्धार (Afghanistan) in the north-west, and included several kingdoms like Madra (Sailkot), कुरु (Delhi), Kekaya (Punjab), Pāñcāla (Bareilly, Kanauj in Uttar Pradesh), कोसल (Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh), Videha (Tirhut in Bihar), Kauśāmbi (Kosam, in Uttar Pradesh) and काशी. The kings who ruled over these countries were all kṣattriyas who were experts in warfare and administration, as also in the Vedic lore. In fact, they were the traditional custodians of some types of esoteric sciences. They not only sheltered learned ब्राह्मणस् and sages but also strove to propagate the Vedic धर्म. They were ruthless in enforcing the highest standards of सत्य (truth) and धर्म (righteousness). The वर्ण system was very much in vogue. As for the आश्रम system, ब्रह्मचर्य, गार्हस्थ्य and वानप्रस्थ were more common, though there is enough reason to believe that सṁन्यास was also being practised. Great stress was laid on the purity and integrity of personal life, irrespective of a person’s station in life.
Apart from religion, एथिच्स् and philosophy, a number of secular sciences like grammar, मुसिच्, dance, archery, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, exorcising the evil spirits, preparing of perfumes, toxicology and so on, were also well-known.
Vedic sacrifices were very common. If they provided an occasion for the kings to earn merit and show their generosity, it was also an opportunity to the scholars to display their knowledge and earn name and fame, as also some wealth.
On the whole, people seemed to be contended with whatever they could earn by the right means. They believed that their sorrows and misfortunes were caused by their own कर्म in their previous lives and hence did not hold others responsible for the same.
9. Literary Grace
The language of the उपनिषद्स् is closely allied to that of the वेदस्. Hence it is not only archaic but also abounds in Vedic phraseology and symbolism.
Most of the उपनिषद्स् are in verses composed in standard Vedic metres. Some like the Māṇḍūkya, the Taittirīya and the Aitareya are completely in prose. Some have a mixture of both.
One of the striking features of the Upaniṣadic literature is its use of beautiful similes and examples. The simile of two birds (the jīvātman and the परमात्मन्) perching on the same tree (the human body) occurs in several उपनिषद्स्: Kaṭha (
