10. Stories
Strangely enough, the उपनिषद्स्, though teaching recondite philosophy, also give us some interesting stories. The Kena describes how the gods in हेअवेन्, under the leadership of इन्द्र, were taught a lesson by ब्रह्मन् in the guise of a यक्ष or demigod (3.1 to 11). A major part of the Kaṭha is devoted to the story of नचिकेतस् and यम. The Chāndogya contains the following stories: Dogs singing the उद्गीथ (1.12); the king जानश्रुति learning from the sage रैक्व (4.1 to 3); the story of Satyakāma Jābāla approaching Hāridrumata for knowledge (4.4 to 9); the story of Satyakāma and his disciple उपकोसल (4.10 to 15); श्वेतकेतु the proud boy, his humble ड़थेर् गौतम and the king प्रवाहण जैवलि (5.3 to 10); Sanatkumāra teaching नारद (7.1 to 26); इन्द्र and विरोचन approaching प्रजापति for the knowledge of the आत्मन् (8.7 to 12).
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka too is not lagging behind. Its stories and legends are: the struggle between the देवस् (gods) and असुरस् (demons) to supersede each other (1.3); the proud बालाकि and the wise king अजातशत्रु (2.1); मैत्रेयी seeking spiritual wisdom from her husband याज्ञवल्क्य (2.4 and 4.5); king जनक and the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य (chapters 3 and 4).
11. Ṛṣis or Sages of the Upaniṣads
We come across a good number of ṛṣis or sages in the उपनिषद्स्. Some like याज्ञवल्क्य are extraordinarily great geniuses. Others like गौतम आरुणि are excellent teachers. A few others like श्वेतकेतु are hard task-masters. Sacrifices conducted by rich and powerful—but noble—kings provided opportunities to these sages not only to exhibit their skills but also earn wealth and fame.
A selected list of sages that occur in the major उपनिषद्स् may now be given just for the sake of information:
Aṅgiras, भृगु, Gārgī, घोर आङ्गिरस, Hāridrumata, Mahidāsa ऐतरेय, नारद, पिप्पलाद, रैक्व, Sanatkumāra, शाण्डिल्य, Satyakāma Jābāla, उद्दालक आरुणि, वामदेव and वरुण.
Yama, the god of death, प्रजापति, the creator, great kings like जनक, अजातशत्रु and प्रवाहण जैवलि also appear in the role of teachers.
One thing that strikes us is that these teachers were revered for their knowledge and excellence, irrespective of their birth, caste or sex.
12. A Résumé of the Principal Upaniṣads
A brief summary of the more ancient and important उपनिषद्स् can now be given here. For the sake of convenience and ready reference, they have been arranged in the English alphabetical order. The details of the Veda to which they belong, the number of chapters, sections and mantras are given in brackets to facilitate better understanding.
AITAREYA UPANIṢAD
(Ṛgveda; 4 chapters; 6 sections; 33 mantras)
One of the more enigmatic of the उपनिषद्स्, this small work gets its name from Mahidāsa ऐतरेय, the son of इतरा. He is the ṛṣi of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka of which this Upaniṣad is a part.
Ātman or परमात्मन्, the supreme Lord, alone existed in the beginning. He desired to create the world and did it without the aid of any other thing, by himself, out of himself. He also entered into that च्रेअतिओन्. This is the gist of the first chapter.
The second chapter describes the birth, the metamorphosis, the death and the rebirth of the jīvātman in order to awaken वैराग्य or detachment in our minds. It is only by realising our real nature as आत्मन् that we become free from the shackles of सṁसार or transmigration. The sage वामदेव succeeded in getting that spiritual wisdom even while in the womb of his मोथेर् and became free.
The last section of the Upaniṣad distinguishes मनस् or the मिन्द् from prajñāna or pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and declares that it is this prajñāna that is the real आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन्, by realising which वामदेव became free.
BṚHADĀRAṆYAKA UPANIṢAD
(Śukla Yajurveda; 6 chapters; 47 sections; 435 mantras)
Considered to be an integral part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the Śukla Yajurveda, this Upaniṣad is the biggest (as its very name suggests) and is quite ancient. It is in prose and contains quotations from other ancient sources which are all in verses.
The first two chapters aim at describing the आत्मन् who is beyond the various Vedic deities. He is the inmost Self of all and is nearest and dearest. A living body is able to function only because of his presence inside. To realise him one has to give up worldly desires, take to the life of a monk or a mendicant and practise meditation on his true nature. Realising him is the same as realising ब्रह्मन्, the cosmic Spirit.
In the third and the fourth chapters we find याज्ञवल्क्य, the genius of a sage, at his best. He not only vanquishes all his opponents but also establishes the fundamental teachings of Vedānta very effectively. A very brief summary of these teachings is as follows: The life of a being here and hereafter is determined by the कर्म he has done—good कर्म producing good results and bad कर्म, bad ones. Even ritualistic karmas, in spite of their being coupled with upāsanās, cannot give मोक्ष or freedom. Only the realisation of the आत्मन्, who is really ब्रह्मन्, who transcends the body-मिन्द् complex, can give freedom from transmigratory existence. To realise this आत्मन्, the wise ब्राह्मणस् renounce their family, wealth and the desire for हेअवेन्, and take to the life of a mendicant.
Yājñavalkya describes that which has pervaded everything in च्रेअतिओन्, which has also transcended it and is also its अन्तर्यामिन् or the inner-controller, as अक्षर (the Indestructible). He gives a long list of its characteristics which appear to be rather self-contradictory or confusing since it is an attempt to describe the indescribable.
He also establishes the true nature of the आत्मन्, by an analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, as the ever free blissful Self.
A description of the जीव suffering at the time of his death and his transmigration also find a place in these teachings, to induce वैराग्य.
The last two chapters contain a number of upāsanās, as on the प्रणव or Oṁ, the need to cultivate the virtues like self-control, compassion and giving gifts to the needy, the Pañcāgnividyā (the doctrine of ड़िवे ड़िरेस्) and some rituals connected with the birth of a son.
The Upaniṣad ends with a long list of the line of the Vedic teachers.
CHĀNDOGYA UPANIṢAD
(Sāmaveda; 8 chapters; 154 sections; 628 mantras)
Considered to be the oldest of the उपनिषद्स्, the Chāndogya begins with the upāsanā on Oṁ as the उद्गीथ, the part of the Sāmaveda sung by the उद्गातृ priest. meditation on Oṁ as प्राण (the life-force) and as the person in the sun are the other topics dealt with in the first chapter.
There are various types of sāmans (mantras of the Sāmaveda). The second chapter recommends several upāsanās on sāmans. There is also a reference to the four āśramas (stages of life) and to the fact that one who is established in ब्रह्मन् attains इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
The third chapter starts with the Madhuvidyā, meditation on the sun as मधु or honey since he gives joy to the gods. meditation on ब्रह्मन् through the गायत्री-मन्त्र is also mentioned here. The famous Śāṇḍilyavidyā is also a part of this chapter. It consists of meditating on the आत्मन् as the creator and sustainer of the universe, in one’s own heart. How a human being can live long is also described by considering one’s life as a long यज्ञ. The example of Mahidāsa ऐतरेय is quoted as the model for such a meditation.
The next chapter starts with the story of the king जानश्रुति Pautrāyaṇa and his attaining wisdom, from the sage रैक्व. Upāsanā on the वायु (air) outside and the प्राण (vital air) inside as the power that absorbs everything into itself is his teaching. It has been called Saṁvarga-vidyā.
A description of the जीव travelling by the Arcirādimārga to the ब्रह्मलोक as a result of meditation on the अक्षिपुरुष or the ‘person in the eye’, who is ब्रह्मन्, also finds a place here.
The fifth chapter delineates the process by which the dead return to this world again. This, as taught by the king प्रवाहण जैवलि to गौतम, is known as Pañcāgnividyā. meditation on the supreme आत्मन्, living inside the body as Vaiśvānarātman, makes one the enjoyer of all ड़ोओद् through all beings. This is the next teaching, given by the king अश्वपति to the five sages who had approached him for knowledge.
The sixth chapter is, by far, the most interesting and instructive. Finding that his son श्वेतकेतु was puffed up with egoism even after his एदुचतिओन् at the गुरु’s होउसे, उद्दालक आरुणि questions him about that by knowing which everything else becomes known. Since श्वेतकेतु was ignorant in this regard, आरुणि starts teaching him in various ways. Before its च्रेअतिओन्, this world was one with Sat (the self-existent Truth). This Sat willed to become many. The world was created out of it in stages. Sat also entered into this world as the jīvātman. आरुणि traces the true nature of the Self through an analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. His final teaching is that श्वेतकेतु in his essential nature is that Sat itself.
The next chapter is in the form of a long dialogue between Sanatkumāra and his disciple नारद. Though नारद had mastered several sciences and arts, he had no peace of मिन्द् since he had not known the आत्मन्. Sanatkumāra takes him step by step through several modes of upāsanās, and finally to भूमन् or ब्रह्मन्.
The last chapter starts with the Daharavidyā, meditation on the Self within the small आकाश of the heart. A major part of this chapter is devoted to the teaching of प्रजापति to इन्द्र, the king of gods, about the आत्मन्, the true Self within. The Upaniṣad concludes with the statement of a liberated सोउल् about his being free from all sins and attaining the world of ब्रह्मन्.
ĪŚĀVĀSYA UPANIṢAD (Śukla Yajurveda; 18 verses)
Though the smallest of the ten major उपनिषद्स्, the Īśāvāsya has attracted the attention of several savants who have chosen to comment upon it. Some of its terms like विद्या and अविद्या, as also sambhūti and asambhūti, have proved to be elusive or vague, thus giving rise several conflicting interpretations.
It teaches that the whole world is pervaded by Īśa or God. It advocates the performance of कर्म or one’s duties and encourages human beings to desire to live the full span of life, viz., one hundred years. After describing the nature of the आत्मन्, it declares that one who has realised this आत्मन् in himself and sees the same in others, transcends sorrow and delusion. It advises the practice of a balanced combination of विद्या (meditation) and अविद्या (karma, sanctioned by the scriptures and helpful to meditation) as also sambhūti (meditation on ब्रह्मन्) and asambhūti (duties to be performed in the world). There is also a beautiful description of परमात्मन् and a prayer for God-vision by the sage at the time of his death.
JĀBĀLA UPANIṢAD (Atharvaveda; 6 chapters; 6 passages)
This is a small Upaniṣad in prose. All the six chapters contain long passages. A description of वाराणसी (the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे) and upāsanā on the space between the eyebrows as वाराणसी is the first teaching given in this Upaniṣad. The जप of the Śatarudrīya-मन्त्र also finds a place in this upāsanā. This is followed by a discourse on सṁन्यास (monkhood) by याज्ञवल्क्य in reply to a query by the king जनक. It includes some details of the procedure also. It concludes with a beautiful description of the way of life of some great men of realisation like Saṁvartaka, आरुणि, Ṛbhu, जडभरत, दत्तात्रेय and others.
KAIVALYA UPANIṢAD (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; 2 chapters; 24 mantras)
This small work is in the form of a dialogue between the sage आश्वलायन (the disciple) and the creator ब्रह्मा (the teacher). It stresses the importance of त्याग or renunciation in the path of knowing ब्रह्मन्. Some details of meditation on ब्रह्मन् in one’s own heart, while sitting in a clean and secluded place, are given. This meditation is compared to the production of fire by the mutual rubbing of the two pieces of अरणि (See ARAṆI), normally used to generate fire in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. This is then followed by the usual description of ब्रह्मन् (as given in other उपनिषद्स्) and the state of realisation of आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन् attained by the aspirant.
KAṬHA UPANIṢAD (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; 6 chapters; 119 mantras)
Also known as Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad, it is an extremely readable and interesting work. It starts with the story of the sage Vājaśśravas performing a sacrifice. Seeing the famished and useless cows kept apart by him to be gifted away during the sacrifice, नचिकेतस्, his young son, tries to draw his attention to this lacuna. Vājaśśravas gets annoyed, and in a fit of anger, curses his son, ‘I give you to Death!’ नचिकेतस् goes straight to the world of यम, the god of death. Finding यम absent, he patiently awaits his return, for three days, not touching ड़ोओद् or water. When यम on returning feels great remorse for having kept a guest outside the होउसे denying even elementary comforts. Of the three boons he grants to नचिकेतस् as atonement, the third is utilised by नचिकेतस् for seeking ātma-ज्ञान or knowledge of the Self. After thoroughly testing the boy with many a tempting offer, यम finally teaches him spiritual wisdom.
Two choices offer themselves before every human being—preyas (the pleasant) and श्रेयस् (the good). Ordinary mortals choose the former and get into endless trouble leading to bondage. The wise ones however, forsake प्रेयस्, the immediately pleasant, for श्रेयस्, the path of spiritual good, which alone can give permanent happiness, peace and bliss.
Realising the आत्मन् is the highest aspect of श्रेयस्. Though the nature of the आत्मन्, the true Self of man, is too subtle to be grasped, it can be properly understood when taught by a competent गुरु or preceptor. Self-control on the one hand, and grace of God on the other, are aids in realising this आत्मन्. यम describes the आत्मन् or the जीव as the master of the chariot, the chariot being the body itself. Just as the master sitting in a good chariot drawn by good horses and an expert driver reaches his destination, so also the जीव reaches the abode of विष्णु if the body and the senses are in good condition and controlled by a wise intellect.
Drawn by the attraction of the senses, a person lets his मिन्द् go outwards. However, if he can withdraw it from the outward objects and direct it within himself, he can realise his आत्मन्.
Yama also declares that the destiny of a being, after his death, is determined by his कर्म or actions done in this life. He compares the created world to an inverted tree, ब्रह्मन् being the root that sustains it. If taught by a competent teacher and through the conquest of desires, one can know this ब्रह्मन्.
Comparing the jīvātman to a person of the size of the thumb and that the exit through the crown of the head at the time of death leads to the abode of ब्रह्मन्, as also comparing the jīvātman and परमात्मन् to two birds perching on the same tree (the body) are the other special aspects of the teaching of this Upaniṣad.
KAUṢĪTAKI UPANIṢAD (Ṛgveda; 4 chapters; 51 mantras)
Also called Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇopa-niṣad, it is a fairly long Upaniṣad and is entirely in prose.
The first chapter deals with the two well-known paths—Devayāna and Pitṛ-yāna. There is a fairly detailed description of not only the journey to the world of ब्रह्मा, by the Arcirādimārga or Deva-yāna, but also of the ब्रह्मलोक itself.
The second chapter gives a detailed account of Prāṇavidyā, upāsanā of प्राण as ब्रह्मन्. There is also a rite recommended to be performed by anyone coveting ‘ekadhana,’ interpreted as the ‘highest wealth’.
The third chapter contains a long discourse by इन्द्र (who has realised the Supreme Being and hence identified with him) to the king प्रतर्दन, the son of दिवोदास. इन्द्र advises प्रतर्दन to meditate on him as प्राण. प्राण is also identified with prajñā (consciousness).
The last chapter which is in the form of a dialogue between the king अजातशत्रु and the learned गार्ग्य बालाकि is almost a repetition of Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.1).
KENA UPANIṢAD (Sāmaveda; 4 chapters; 35 mantras)
Also known as Talavakāra Upaniṣad, this small work gets its name by its very first word ‘kena’ (‘by what’). The first half is in verses and the second half in prose.
The Upaniṣad begins with a description of the आत्मन् in the body as the spirit behind the sense-organs and the मिन्द्. It has been identified with ब्रह्मन्. Though it cannot be known as an object, since it is the subject, its presence is felt in and through every thought. When this real seer is realised, a person becomes immortal.
The second section gives the parable of the gods in हेअवेन्. Under the leadership of इन्द्र they had met to celebrate their victory over the असुरस् or demons forgetting that it was due to the grace and power of ब्रह्मन् and not to their own valour. ब्रह्मन् appeared on the scene as a यक्ष (a demi-god) and taught them a lesson after humiliating them. Then Umā हैमवती (the personification of ब्रह्मविद्या) came on the scene and taught इन्द्र, spiritual wisdom.
The Upaniṣad specially mentions that तपस् (austerity), दम (self-control) and कर्म (actions ordained by the scriptures) are the basic disciplines needed to attain knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. It concludes with a eulogy of this knowledge.
MAHĀNĀRĀYAṆA UPANIṢAD (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; 80 sections; 259 mantras)
The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda contains two well-known उपनिषद्स्: the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad. The latter is also known as the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad and the Yājñikī Upaniṣad.
Two recensions are available now: the Āndhrapāṭha and the Drāviḍapāṭha, the former being the longer one.
This Upaniṣad seems to be a composition of many varied subjects, almost like an appendix or an addenda to some other work. There is no systematic treatment of any major doctrine. Each section seems to be an independent unit. It deals with all the three aspects of Vedic religion viz., कर्म (rituals), ज्ञान (knowledge) and upāsanā (meditation).
Some of the most popular of the Vedic sūktas which are chanted even now during religious ceremonies—like the Nārāyaṇa-sūkta, the Durgāsūkta and the Medhā-sūkta—find a place here.
The mantras commonly used during the सन्ध्या rituals, mantras used during saṁnyāsadīkṣā (taking to the monastic order), several गायत्री hymns on different deities and some famous mantras like the त्रिसुपर्णमन्त्रस् also find a prominent place.
Various aspects of spiritual life like सत्य (truth), तपस् (austerity), दम (sense-control), दान (giving gifts), धर्म (righteous living) and शम (mental peace) have been greatly stressed.
A beautiful description of the Cosmic Person in the orb of the sun, contemplation on the various parts of a यज्ञ or sacrifice in a symbolical way and the journey to the ब्रह्मलोक are also included among the topics dealt with by this Upaniṣad.
MĀṆḌŪKYA UPANIṢAD (Atharvaveda; 12 mantras)
Comprising only 12 mantras—all in prose—this small Upaniṣad delves straight-away into the philosophy of प्रणव (Oṁ), आत्मन् and ब्रह्मन्. प्रणव is the best symbol of the eternal truth, ब्रह्मन्. The आत्मन् inside this body—whose existence and real nature are established by this Upaniṣad through the analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, viz., जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state) and सुषुप्ति (deep sleep state)—and ब्रह्मन्, the Cosmic Truth are, in the ultimate analysis, one and the same. He is called the तुरीय (the Fourth, beyond the three states described). It is impossible to describe his nature since he is acintya (beyond thought) and alakṣaṇa (beyond characteristics). He alone has to be known. meditation on the प्रणव (Oṁ), especially its last part, results in the realisation of the आत्मन्.
A long commentary called Kārikā (in verses) attributed to गौडपाद (circa A.

), generally goes with it and is studied deeply by the students of Vedānta.
MUṆḌAKA UPANIṢAD (Atharvaveda; 3 chapters; 6 sections; 64 mantras)
The word ‘muṇḍa’ means a shaven head. This Upaniṣad might have derived its name from the fact that the spiritual wisdom contained in it can shave off all the illusions and delusions of one who studies it and understands it. Or, it could be that it was specially meant for the saṁnyāsins with shaven heads.
Cast in excellent poetry, this Upaniṣad is a delight to read.
It divides all knowledge into two groups—the parā (higher) and the aparā (lower). Except the knowledge of the अक्षर, the indestructible ब्रह्मन्, all other branches of knowledge—including the वेदस् themselves—are only अपरा-विद्या, lower or inferior knowledge! Then comes a nice description of this अक्षर-ब्रह्मन् and the च्रेअतिओन् of the world out of it.
Though Vedic rituals were considered necessary and sacred, this Upaniṣad points out their limitations and advises the aspirant after spiritual wisdom to eschew them like leaky rafters, take to a life of renunciation and approach a competent गुरु for ब्रह्मविद्या or knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. The method of meditation on ब्रह्मन् with the help of प्रणव (Oṁ) is picturesquely described with the simile of a bow and arrow. This ends in the realisation of the आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन् inside oneself, thereby resulting in the destruction of all the knots of इग्नोरन्चे that bind one’s heart or being.
The work compares the jīvātman and the परमात्मन् to two birds perching on the same tree, which is this body. The former is bound whereas the latter is ever free. However, when he realises this परमात्मन् he goes beyond good and evil and attains union with him.
The famous declaration that Truth alone triumphs and not falsehood (vide

) belongs to this Upaniṣad.
This आत्मन् can be realised only when taught by an enlightened preceptor and never by merely listening to discourses or intellectualism. However, the grace of God plays a very important part in this realisation.
Both types of liberation—the gradual one by going to the ब्रह्मलोक and the instantaneous one, at the fall of the body—have been mentioned towards the end of this Upaniṣad.
PRAŚNA UPANIṢAD (Atharva-veda; 6 chapters; 67 mantras)
Since the Upaniṣad is in the form of praśnas or questions and their answers, it has been named as Praśnopaniṣad.
Six sages like Kabandhi कात्यायन, भार्गव Vaidarbhi and others, come to the great teacher पिप्पलाद with their questions. After they undergo the disciplines of student-hood for one year—as per his command—they approach him again, with six questions. The answers provided by पिप्पलाद form the main body of this work.
The first section deals with the subject: What is the origin of all the beings? पिप्पलाद describes it as प्रजापति (God, as the Lord of all beings), who creates the universe through the combination of rayi (Soma or matter) and प्राण (Agni or आदित्य or Spirit). There is also a mention of the two paths: उत्तरायण (the Northern Path) and दक्षिणायन (the Southern Path).
The second section describes the mukhyaprāṇa (the main life force) as the sole support of the body and the sense-organs.
The third section says that this mukhyaprāṇa emerges out of the Parama-पुरुष or the Cosmic Person (God). He works inside this body in five forms. At the time of death, the udānavāyu (one of the five forms of mukhya-प्राण) carries the जीव through one of the nāḍīs (a tubular path for the flow of prāṇic energy) originating in the heart, to हेअवेन् or हेल्ल् or this very world of human beings, depending upon his कर्म.
The fourth section gives an account of the deep sleep state of a being. In that state, the जीव is merged in परमात्मन् or the Supreme Self.
The next section delineates the method of meditation on the प्रणव (Oṁ) and the results one obtains from it. Highest meditation leads to the attainment of ब्रह्मलोक.
The last section, the sixth, deals with the ṣoḍaśakalapuruṣa, ‘the person with sixteen parts’. He is the jīvātman. When these so-called parts get destroyed, the jīvātman becomes immortal.
ŚVETĀŚVATARA UPANIṢAD (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; 6 chapters; 113 mantras)
This Upaniṣad starts with a discussion by some sages on the jagatkāraṇa or the ultimate cause of this world, and comes to the conclusion, in the very first chapter, that the Devātmaśakti or the परमात्मन् (God) with his inherent power, is that cause. This truth is discovered by them through ध्यानयोग or meditation. This is followed by a description of jīvātman and परमात्मन् through various elegant phrases.
The second chapter deals with the योग of meditation, the various aids to meditation like control and concentration of the मिन्द्, the right posture, प्राणायाम or regulation of the prāṇic energy through breath-control and some results of the practice of योग.
The third chapter contains several mantras found in other Vedic sections like the Rudrādhyāya and the Puruṣasūkta. The descriptions, again, centre round the jīvātman and the परमात्मन्.
Continuing the same subject, the next chapter declares that those who realise the truth, ब्रह्मन्, will attain इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
The fifth chapter deals with the emergence of हिरण्यगर्भ (the Golden-egg or the Cosmic Person) (called ‘Kapila’ here) from परमेश्वर, the Supreme Lord. Descriptions of several aspects of च्रेअतिओन् are also there. That the आत्मन् (Brahman) can be known through the secret parts of the Veda and that the knowers of the same attain इम्मोर्तलित्य् is repeated here.
The sixth and the last chapter declares परमेश्वर or the Supreme Lord as the lord of the karmas of the individual souls, and also eulogises his greatness. The teachings of such उपनिषद्स् as this are revealed only to those who have devotion not only to परमेश्वर but also to the गुरु or spiritual teacher—is another important declaration of this Upaniṣad.
TAITTIRĪYA UPANIṢAD (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; 3 chapters; 31 mantras)
The three chapters of this Upaniṣad are respectively called Śīkṣāvallī, ब्रह्मा-nandavallī and Bhṛguvallī, based on the first words used in them.
The first chapter starts with the science of शिक्षा or phonetics. This is then followed by certain meditations on such subjects as jyotis or light and a few homas (ceremonial oblations into fire) meant for persons desirous of wealth and intelligence. meditation on ब्रह्मन् within oneself, through the व्याहृतिस् like bhū etc., is also touched upon. The last part gives the parting message of the Vedic teacher to his student who is about to leave the institution.
The second chapter describes the five kośas or sheaths that cover the आत्मन्, like the annamaya (the sheath of ड़ोओद्, viz., the body), the prāṇamaya (the sheath of sense-organs) and so on. There is also an interesting attempt to show that the bliss of realising ब्रह्मन् is infinitely superior to the pleasures one gets at the lower levels (in this world or in हेअवेन्) by taking the ideal human happiness as the basic unit.
The last chapter extols तपस् or austerity as the means of realising ब्रह्मन् and also describes some upāsanās on अन्न or ड़ोओद्. That one should not despise ड़ोओद् in any way, that one should honour guests with ड़ोओद् and shelter, is another idea prominently taught here. The Upaniṣad ends with the declaration that one who transcends the five sheaths and realises the आत्मन्, who is also in the sun, attains eternal joy.
VAJRASŪCIKĀ UPANIṢAD (Sāmaveda; 9 mantras)
This is a small Upaniṣad in prose, except for the first मन्त्र. It asks the question, ‘Who is a ब्राह्मण?’ and answers it.
The body, the individual सोउल्, birth, knowledge, work, religious duties—none of these makes one a ब्राह्मण. It is character that makes a person a real ब्राह्मण.
One who has realised the Self, the one without a second, who is therefore free from all faults and defects, is a real ब्राह्मण. Peace of मिन्द्, and absence of desire, jealousy and delusion, as also egotism, are his characteristics.
The text closes with the exhortation to one and all to become a true ब्राह्मण by realising ब्रह्मन्.
13. Conclusion
The उपनिषद्स् contain the quintessence of Vedic religion and philosophy. The Ṣaḍdarśanas or the six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् derive their strength and inspiration from them. The Vedānta systems are entirely an outcome of their study. The idea of मोक्ष as the primary goal of life, which has permeated the Indian religions and culture of the succeeding centuries, owes its origin entirely to the उपनिषद्स्. And, they are the basis of the प्रस्थानत्रय (the three foundational scriptures), the other two being the Bhagavadgītā and the Brahma-sūtras.
The depth as well as the catholicity of their thought has attracted the attention of the savants of other religions and societies also, resulting in their being translated into other languages too.
An earnest study of the उपनिषद्स्, without preconceived notions and prejudices, is bound to inspire one to aspire for the life of the spirit.

upavīta
------------------------------------------
Every द्विज (‘the twice-born,’ a member of the first three varṇas or castes) is expected to undergo the sacrament of उपनयन and wear the यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) on his body always. The normal and permanent way of wearing it is to put it on the left shoulder and allow it to hang below the right armpit. This mode of wearing is called उपवीत.
For other modes see NIVĪTA.

Upamanyu
------------------------------------------
Upamanyu was a disciple of the sage धौम्य. He was entrusted with the task of taking care of his गुरु’s cows. Once he felt very hungry and had nothing to eat. He ate the leaves of a poisonous shrub which made him lose his eye-sight. Not knowing the way to return, he fell into a dry well. There, he prayed to the twin deities, the अश्विन्स् and regained his eyesight (vide महाभारत, Ādiparva 3).
The Liṅgapurāṇa (107) gives the story of another उपमन्यु, the son of the sage Vyāghrapāda. As a little boy, he pestered his मोथेर् for milk. Due to extreme poverty, the मोथेर् gave him some water mixed with a little flour since there was no milk. The boy refused to drink it. As advised by the मोथेर्, he prayed to शिव and got the rulership over the ocean of milk! It was he who composed a Śivasahasranāma.

upasthāna
(‘worship or homage’)
------------------------------------------
An आहिताग्नि (one who has ceremonially established the Vedic fires) is expected to perform अग्निहोत्र (See AGNIHOTRA for details.) both in the morning and in the evening. After the evening offering he is expected to pay homage to the fire by reciting the Vātsapra mantras (vide Ṛgveda 10.45; Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā 3.11.36; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa

.9-41). This is called उपस्थान.
Whether this उपस्थान should be done only in the evening or both in the morning and in the evening, opinion seems to be divided.

upavasatha
(‘to dwell near,’ ‘to fast’)
------------------------------------------
A Vedic sacrificer is expected to fast and keep vigil before beginning the main rite. This ड़स्तिन्ग् as also the day of ड़स्तिन्ग् is known as उपवसथ. On this day, preliminary matters like preparation of an altar, fetching of the यूप (sacrificial post) etc., are attended to.

upāya
(‘means or method’)
------------------------------------------
This is a general term with several shades of meaning. It can mean any method by which we can attain what we want.
According to one version, it can be classified as laukika (secular) and alaukika (non-secular or spiritual). The wheel and the stick used in preparing a mud-pot are laukika-upāyas. Performing a sacrifice like the ज्योतिष्टोम to attain हेअवेन् is अलौकिक-उपाय.
A king has to use one of the four prescribed upāyas in subduing or getting rid of his enemies. They are: sāma (negotiation by peaceful means); दान (a policy of give and take); bheda (manoeuvring a split in the enemy ranks); दण्ड (warfare, fighting).
A creditor can get back his money from the debtor by using any of the following upāyas: धर्म (by negotiation through mutual friends and well-wishers); vyavahāra (by helping the debtor to establish himself in a profitable job and get back his money when he prospers); balātkāra (by forcibly taking away the debtor’s property).
In certain schools of शैविस्म्, five upāyas are recommended for spiritual progress. They are: vāsacaryā (leading a pure life); जप (repetition of divine name); ध्यान (meditation); rudrasmaraṇa (remembering Lord रुद्र or शिव); प्रपत्ति (surrender to God).

Upavarṣa
------------------------------------------
The principal schools of Vedānta are based on their interpretation of the Brahmasūtras of बादरायण. The pioneering ācāryas (teachers) of these schools often try to garner support for their philosophy from the earlier, more ancient, teachers, who might have commented upon it. One such, quoted by Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) is the वृत्ति-kāra बोधायन. शङ्कर (A.
-820) refers to one उपवर्ष. According to वेदान्त देशिक (A.

-1370) both are the same person.
Upavarṣa had two more names, Kṛtakoṭi and Halabhūti.
Nothing is known about him.
According to some scholars he wrote a commentary on the Pūrvamīmāṁsā Sūtras and existed during the period 100 B. C. and A.

uparati
(‘cessation’)
------------------------------------------
Advaita Vedānta prescribes a fourfold spiritual discipline, called साधनचतुष्टय, as a preliminary step. Śamādi-ṣaṭka forms the third step of this discipline.
Śamādiṣaṭka comprises a group of six exercises viz., शम (tranquillity), दम (control of external sense-organs), उपरति (cessation), तितिक्षा (forbearance), श्रद्धा (faith) and समाधान (concentration).
Uparati is the cessation of the sense-organs, after they are restrained, from the pursuit of sense-objects.

upādhi
(‘limiting adjunct’)
------------------------------------------
Any adventitious object which apparently influences something else to appear differently from what it really is, is ‘upādhi’. For instance, a red flower near a colourless crystal makes it appear as red. The red flower is called an ‘upādhi’ for the crystal. Similarly the body-मिन्द् complex is an उपाधि for the आत्मन् (the individual सोउल्) making it appear as the जीव (the limited transmigrating self) and the world is an उपाधि for ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, who has nothing to do with च्रेअतिओन्.

upaśruti
(‘oracular voices’)
------------------------------------------
Upaśruti is a curious mode of divining the future, described in some works on prognostication.
One of the methods prescribes that three married woman along with a maiden, should worship an image of गणेश as per the rules given in such works, keep it in front of the होउसे of a washerman or an outcaste in the early morning and listen attentively to the conversations in the होउसे uttered freely. A proper analysis of this can lead to the solution of the problem on hand.
